beats.title: A Database Column's Nullability Is Changed
beats.body: A pull request removes the ability for a due-date column to store null values, enforcing that every document record must carry a due date. The change is motivated by the observation that invoices and bills always require a due date at the frontend, making a non-null constraint seem like the correct data-integrity rule.

beats.title: Strict Constraint vs. Flexible Schema for Optional Fields
beats.body: Enforcing a non-null constraint improves data integrity for the common case but breaks document types—such as credit and debit notes—that legitimately have no due date. The team must choose between a strict schema that reflects the majority use case and a permissive schema that accommodates all document variants without workarounds.

beats.title: Position A — pavel-mironchik
beats.body: The nullable column was likely introduced deliberately to support document types that have no due date concept. Making it non-null would break existing data migrations and force modules to supply a meaningless placeholder date just to satisfy the constraint, which is a semantic hack rather than a real fix.
beats.author: pavel-mironchik

beats.title: Position B — burakcakirel
beats.body: The non-null constraint is the correct long-term rule for invoices and bills, and the nullable state was an oversight. The migration script can be updated to handle legacy records, and modules without a due date can supply a sentinel value through a hidden field to satisfy validation without changing the schema design.
beats.author: burakcakirel

beats.question: Given the risk to existing data migrations and the need to support document types without due dates, would you enforce the non-null constraint, keep the column nullable, or pursue a different approach entirely?
